props.title: A Man Vanishes

sections.content: **A Man Vanishes (1967)** (1967) revolutionized documentary filmmaking by deliberately blurring reality and fiction. Director Shohei Imamura started making what appeared to be a straightforward documentary about Japan's epidemic of disappearing citizens, focusing on Tadashi Oshima, a plastics salesman who vanished in 1965. But Imamura's approach became increasingly experimental, having his crew interact on camera and eventually revealing artificial studio sets. This groundbreaking technique influenced later works like **F for Fake** (1973) and **Close-Up** (1990), establishing a new form of hybrid documentary that questions the very nature of truth in cinema.

sections.content: Imamura's radical departure from traditional documentary form came at a crucial moment in Japanese cinema. While the Japanese New Wave was deconstructing narrative fiction through films like **Death by Hanging** (1968) and **The Man Who Left His Will on Film** (1970), Imamura attacked documentary's claim to objective truth. His revelation that the missing man's fiancée had become romantically involved with a crew member during filming transforms **A Man Vanishes** into a meditation on performance, reality, and the impossibility of capturing unfiltered truth. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Documentary

The film's influence resonates through contemporary hybrid documentaries like **The Act of Killing** (2012) and **Stories We Tell** (2012), which similarly employ dramatic reconstructions and self-reflexive techniques. Imamura's pioneering work opened new possibilities for documentary filmmakers to acknowledge their own role in shaping reality. **Exit Through the Gift Shop** (2010) and **Casting JonBenet** (2017) follow this tradition, using unreliable narrators and multiple perspectives to question documentary authenticity.
